titleStmt.title: No. 928
Memorandum by the Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs (Jernegan) to the Secretary of State

div.head:
No. 928
Memorandum by the Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs (Jernegan) to the Secretary of State
div.p:
Attached is a study, for use at the meeting with you on December 10, setting forth our preliminary views on how a final Arab-Israel settlement might be approached. We are preparing staff papers on specific aspects of the problem such as a security undertaking, frontier rectifications, Jerusalem, repatriation and resettlement
of refugees, role of the United Nations, the price to the United States, etc.

It is our thought that after the meeting with you a definitive staff study would be drawn up. The study would then be used for the discussions with the United Kingdom in London which we suggest should take place about the middle of January.

The attached memorandum should be considered in conjunction with the Talking Paper for your conversation with Sir Anthony Eden on December 16. This memorandum is, in effect, a summary of our present thinking on an Arab-Israel settlement. The Talking Paper deals more with the tactics you may wish to employ in your conversation with Sir Anthony.

Although concentrated re-examination confirms the complexities of the Arab-Israel problem and the fundamentally divergent interests which must be reconciled, the early months of 1955 appear as propitious a period to attempt a settlement as is likely to occur in the foreseeable future. This determination has been made with due recognition of the statement in the latest NIE estimate that the Arab states “will probably not be willing for some time to risk negotiation and compromise on the most important issues” with Israel. Secrecy is an essential element in such an approach. The leaders of the countries involved must be able to study our proposals carefully and with due deliberation. Premature public disclosure will only result in the public repudiation of any desire to seek a settlement. Furthermore, a breach of security could seriously endanger the now promising chances for the success of the negotiations for the unified development of the Jordan watershed—a major ingredient in any overall settlement.

Our study indicates that the best prospects for moving in a span of about two years from the present armistice agreements to formal peace are afforded by combining our present step-by-step approach with an across-the-board effort directed originally at securing an Egyptian-Israel agreement and then a Jordan-Israel agreement, utilizing the Trieste technique. An illustrative timetable covering the first phase of our effort would read: (1) development with the United Kingdom of the elements of a solution and agreement on strategy—January–February 1955; (2) discussions with Turkey, concentrating on the part we hope it will play in the concurrent approach to Middle East defense arrangements—February,
1955; (3) frank and full discussions with Prime Minister Nasir of Egypt—March–April, 1955; (4) depending on Nasir’s receptivity, discussions with Israel—April, 1955. Contingent, to a certain extent, on developments in reconciling the Israel and Egyptian positions, the initial approaches might be made to Jordan and possibly Lebanon while negotiations for an Egypt-Israel settlement were going forward.

We believe the first approach should be made to Egypt because: (a) she is less concerned over Israel and more likely to move; (b) her example, as in the case of Bunche’s negotiations of the armistice agreements at Rhodes, would help induce the other Arab states to act; (c) the Suez Base Agreement and our aid programs place the United States and United Kingdom in a particularly favorable position to influence Egypt; (d) simultaneous approaches to several Arab states would considerably increase the danger of publicity and of the Arabs uniting on an extreme stand.

Among the specific objectives we could hope to achieve at an optimum are: formal peace between Israel and Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon (Syria, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and perhaps Iraq may prove more intractable); permanent boundaries for Israel after frontier rectifications; termination of the Suez Canal blockade and of efforts by the Arab states to enforce a secondary boycott; agreements on repatriation and resettlement of refugees with some implementation; agreements on compensation to the refugees; greater security along Israel’s borders; a Jerusalem settlement; certain transit rights for the Arab states through Israel. If successful, we would still be faced with implementing certain of the agreements reached, particularly those concerned with the refugees.

Concurrently, we would endeavor to progress on area defense arrangements through a series of bilaterals linking certain Arab states to Turkey and Pakistan. Success would contribute to an Arab-Israel settlement by instilling in the Arab states a greater sense of security and by deflecting their concentration on Israel. Israel should eventually be linked to the defense arrangements possibly through a bilateral agreement with Turkey. It would be overly optimistic, however to hope that Israel’s integration into the defense arrangements could take place within the two year period under discussion.

Within the limitations of our Constitutional processes, agreement on a government level should be sought beforehand on the following: (1) continuation of the present policy of impartiality; (2) a firm public undertaking to be given as part of a final settlement, and only in such a context, that the United States would take effective concerted action with the United Kingdom, France and Turkey both in and outside the United Nations, in the event of an armed
attack by Israel or the Arab states on the other—such an undertaking is practically a sine qua non to breaking the psychological log jam which now prevents peace; (3) grant economic assistance to the Arab states and Israel expanded in some cases plus continued aid to the refugees; (4) a program of grant military assistance to certain Arab states and also some military assistance at the appropriate time to Israel.
France should not be associated with the initial undertaking, and should not be informed of the plan at least until after the approach to Egypt.

(NEA hopes that Francis Russell, who is due in the United States next week, may be assigned to work out our thinking on this problem. We hope he could have the aid and guidance of Ray Hare. We think that Russell and/or Hare should probably make the trip to London in January.)

note.p: At this point in the source text, an unknown hand inserted the following: “4:30”.

On Dec. 9, Jernegan received a copy of the preliminary draft of a document entitled “Staff Study-Arab-Israel Settlement” from Parker T. Hart, Director of the Office of Near Eastern Affairs. (NEA files, lot 59 D 518, “Washington Talks, Jan.-Feb. 1955: Memos, etc. preceding actual meetings (Dated 11/15/54 thru 1/27/55)”
